newsitem.title: JAPAN: Forex intervention best when unexpected - Sakakibara.
newsitem.headline: Forex intervention best when unexpected - Sakakibara.

text.p: Intervention to halt excessive currency movements is most effective when it is done at a time when markets do not expect it, senior Ministry of Finance (MOF) official Eisuke Sakakibara said on Friday.
"We don't want to conduct defensive intervention," Sakakibara, director-general of the ministry's International Finance Bureau, told Reuters in an interview.
"I am concerned about the yen's recent movements, which have been very rapid. Recent currency movements cannot be justified by economic fundamentals," he said.
Cooperation among the Group of Seven (G7) industrial nations, which was confirmed at their meeting in February in Berlin, remains unchanged, he said.
"It happened that the United States shares our concern about the yen's recent movements," he said.
"We will not take any actions that could be detected by markets in advance," he said.

Asked about a capital outflow from Japan that has been believed to be buoying the dollar against the yen, Sakakibara said: "Japan turned a net capital importer for February and March as Japanese investors took profits on foreign bonds and repatriated the proceeds, while foreign capital kept flowing into Japan."
Japanese institutional investors may gradually boost the foreign bond weighting in their portfolios, Sakakibara said in the interview, broadcast on Reuters Financial Television.
However, the impact of this on foreign exchange is hard to determine as the investors may decide to hedge against the risks of holding those foreign assets, he said.
Meanwhile, a large amount of foreign bond buying by individual investors is unlikely to continue, he added.

Sakakibara also said that brokerage houses which are actively selling foreign bonds and dual currency bonds to investors should properly explain the inherent dangers in investing in such risky assets.
Sakakibara also said that the Japanese government bond market is considerably "bubbly" and he sees the risk of a bursting of the bubble.
"If I put it rather harshly, the JGB market is considerably bubbly, and there is the risk of a bursting (of the bubble)," Sakakibara said in the interview.

Financial markets generally think the Japanese economy is not good, he said. "However, economic data on the April-June quarter is likely to show an improvement in the economy...(and if markets do not realise this) there would be a surprise."
"I am saying that markets must be very careful. If you analyse carefully, you find there are no indicators showing the economy is worsening," he said.
On interest rates, Sakakibara said it would be natural for the Bank of Japan (BOJ) to raise interest rates when it has confirmed the strength of the economy.
He said it would be dangerous for financial markets to assume that Japan will not raise rates within the next year.
"Current interest rate levels are abnormal and it would be natural if those levels were to be normalised in the future," he said.

Asked what demerits a rise in Japan's interest rates would produce, Sakakibara said the operating profits of Japanese banks would not drop even if short-term interest rates were to be raised by 0.25 or 0.5 percentage point.

"It's entirely up to the BOJ to consider a change in its monetary policy. But raising interest rates would be a natural action for the BOJ to take when it has confirmed the strength of the economy," he said in the interview.

He said there are many people who are dissatisfied with current interest rate levels. "The political mood (about interest rates) can be a factor (in considering a change in Japan's monetary policy)," he said.
"It would be dangerous to assume that Japan will definitely not raise interest rates for the next 12 months," he said.
On Japanese economic growth, Sakakibara said growth is likely to exceed two percent in the current 1997/98 fiscal year after having likely reached nearly three percent in 1996/97.
These forecasts are higher than the government's official targets of 2.5 percent growth for 1996/97, which ended on March 31, and 1.9 percent for 1997/98.
"The possibility of the Japanese economy contracting is less than people think," Sakakibara said.

He said an increase in Japan's sales tax to five percent from three percent on April 1 and the scrapping of special income tax cuts in the current fiscal year did not seem to be having a negative impact on overall consumption.
Real estate prices are likely to rebound, he said.
"The peak of the problem of non-performing loans is over. It looks like major Japanese banks can dispose of problem loans within the next two to three years," he said.
"It is irrational to think that the Japanese economy is going to plunge... At the moment, the upside risk for the Japanese economy is bigger than the downside risk," he said.
Sakakibara also said Japan's surplus in trade of goods and services is likely to fall over the medium and long terms.
"The surplus now accounts for 0.5 percent of Japan's GDP (gross domestic product) and the ratio is the smallest among the Group of Seven (G7) countries which enjoy a surplus," he said.
His remarks about the trade surplus come amid fears of rising trade friction with the United States after U.S. officials expressed concern about an increase in the Japanese surplus.

"The surplus in goods and services trade is not likely to increase substantially in 1997/98, although there could be some deviation from the trend in individual months," he said. Yoshiko Mori - Tokyo Treasury Desk +81-3-3432-8676
